blocks.content: Every operating system has a heart, and that heart is the kernel. It is the one piece of software that is always running, always in control, and trusted with the entire machine. When people talk about what an operating system truly is at its core, they are talking about the kernel.

If you understand the kernel, the rest of the operating system falls into place. It is the part that talks to the hardware, guards the boundary around it, and gives every other program a safe way to get work done.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408308945-620169687.png
1. What the Kernel Is

The kernel is the central program of the operating system. It loads early during boot, stays in memory the whole time the machine is on, and remains in charge until you shut down. Everything else runs on top of it.

Its defining trait is trust. The kernel runs with full privileges over the hardware, which no ordinary program is allowed to have. Because of this power, kernel code is kept small and carefully guarded, since a mistake here can affect the entire system.

blocks.title: The core of the core
blocks.content: If the operating system is the manager of the machine, the kernel is that manager brain and hands. It is the part actually holding the controls, while everything else asks it to act on their behalf.
2. Why a Kernel Is Needed

Imagine if every program could touch the hardware directly. One program could grab all the memory, another could scribble over a third program data, and a single bug could crash the whole machine. There would be no safety and no fairness.

The kernel exists to prevent exactly this. By being the single trusted layer that controls the hardware, it can share resources fairly and keep programs from harming each other. Programs give up direct access in exchange for a safe, orderly system.

blocks.content: 3. What the Kernel Does
The kernel carries out the core jobs that keep the machine running. These are the responsibilities too important and too privileged to trust to any ordinary program.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408308945-134112431.png

It schedules the processor among competing programs, manages how memory is handed out and protected, drives the hardware through device drivers, and handles the system calls through which programs ask for its help. Every one of these touches the hardware or the safety of the system, which is why the kernel owns them.
["Schedules the processor among competing programs","Manages and protects memory","Drives the hardware through device drivers","Handles system calls from programs"]
items: Schedules the processor among competing programs
Manages and protects memory
Drives the hardware through device drivers
Handles system calls from programs

blocks.content: 4. User Mode and Kernel Mode
To enforce its authority, the processor itself supports two modes of running code. This hardware feature is what makes the kernel power real rather than just a promise.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408308946-69278082.png

Ordinary programs run in user mode, where dangerous instructions and direct hardware access are blocked. The kernel runs in kernel mode, with full privileges. When a program needs something privileged, the processor switches into kernel mode to run the kernel, then switches back. The wall between the two is enforced by the hardware.
["The processor supports user mode and kernel mode","Programs run in restricted user mode","The kernel runs in privileged kernel mode","The hardware enforces the wall between them"]
items: The processor supports user mode and kernel mode
Programs run in restricted user mode
The kernel runs in privileged kernel mode
The hardware enforces the wall between them

blocks.title: Two sets of keys
blocks.content: User mode is like a guest key that opens only the guest rooms. Kernel mode is the master key that opens everything. The hardware makes sure guests can never quietly pick up the master key.
5. How Programs Reach the Kernel

Since programs run in restricted user mode, they cannot do privileged work themselves. When they need it, they ask the kernel through a system call, the controlled request that crosses from user mode into kernel mode.

The program makes the request, the processor switches into kernel mode, the kernel checks that the request is allowed and carries it out, then control returns to the program. This is the only sanctioned path in, which is exactly what lets the kernel stay in control of everything privileged.
["Programs in user mode cannot do privileged work directly","They ask the kernel through a system call","The kernel checks the request and carries it out","Control then returns to the program"]
items: Programs in user mode cannot do privileged work directly
They ask the kernel through a system call
The kernel checks the request and carries it out
Control then returns to the program

blocks.title: Ask, do not take
blocks.content: A program never reaches over and grabs the hardware. It politely asks the kernel, which checks the request and does it if allowed. Ask, do not take, is the rule that keeps the system safe.
6. Kernel Space and User Space
The two modes come with a matching split in memory. Kernel space is the protected region where the kernel code and data live, and user space is where all ordinary programs live.

A program in user space cannot read or write kernel space, and it cannot reach into another program memory either. This separation is why one crashing app does not take down the system, and why a bug in your program cannot corrupt the kernel. The kernel guards its own space fiercely.
["Kernel space holds the protected kernel code and data","User space is where ordinary programs run","Programs cannot read or write kernel space","This separation keeps crashes and bugs contained"]

blocks.content: 7. Kernel Designs
Kernels are not all built the same way. The central design question is how much to put inside the kernel, and the answer splits kernels into a few families.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408308946-427635714.png

A monolithic kernel puts most services, including drivers and the file system, inside the kernel, which is fast but means more code runs with full privileges. A microkernel keeps only the bare minimum in the kernel and runs the rest as ordinary programs, which is safer but slower. A hybrid blends the two, and is what most everyday systems actually use.

8. The Kernel Is Not the Whole OS
blocks.text: 8. The Kernel Is Not the Whole OS

blocks.content: It is a common mix up to think the kernel is the entire operating system. It is the core, but a full operating system includes much more around it.

Around the kernel sit the system libraries, the shell or graphical desktop, and the many utility programs and services that make the system pleasant to use. The kernel is the essential foundation, but the operating system is the kernel plus all of this surrounding software working together.

blocks.content: 9. Seeing the Kernel in Action

You rarely notice the kernel, but it is working constantly. Every time you open a file, the kernel checks your permissions and fetches the data. Every time two programs run together, the kernel is switching the processor between them thousands of times a second.

When you plug in a device and it just works, the kernel loaded the right driver. When a program crashes but the rest of your machine keeps running, that is the kernel protection keeping the damage contained. The kernel is the quiet, constant hand behind everything the machine does.

["The kernel works constantly, even when unnoticed","It checks permissions and fetches data on every file access","It switches the processor between programs thousands of times a second","It contains a crash so the rest of the machine keeps running"]
